name: Omar Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and operate a machine that braids steel wire around rubber pressure hose. My vocational certificate covered tension and safe stops; I like cutting a clean test hose, but a snapped wire reel makes a nasty mess. I'm experienced, though I still ask the setter about a tricky coupling.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a library. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and four months of expenses saved. The hose job pays an ordinary operator rate and there are some similar factories nearby. I never use AI tools; I keep gauge readings on paper and go to our union branch meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the braiding crew that the hose still needs tension checked when the computer's order list is wrong. A little AI in the office doesn't change the machine in front of us. I'd raise the same safety point at our union branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is ordinary for this trade, my partner's library wage is regular, and we have four months of expenses saved. We still have two school-age children and a mortgage, but the hose orders are steady and there are some similar factories nearby. I am comfortable with the current shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting braid tension and checking a cut hose sample at each changeover. At the next branch meeting I'll bring the frayed sample from last week and ask that paid checking time stays in the shift target. I never use AI tools and don't need one to show a split sleeve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The family budget works as it is, and I know the line and the people beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the frayed sample show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The steel wire sleeve had opened beside a coupling, where you can miss it under rubber. We stopped the reel and cut another sample before shipping it. A hose that splits at the coupling can ruin a machine far from our factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the family use the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I keep the four-month reserve for a genuine gap in wages or a big repair. This month's pay covers the mortgage, food and school buses. We would draw on that reserve if the van needed work or one of us lost hours.

say: A **braided hose** still needs tension and coupling checks despite a tidier order list.
I will ask our **union branch** to protect paid checking time.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and two wages cover ordinary household costs.
Some **nearby factories** offer options if current hose orders change.
do: **Keep** setting braid tension and cutting test hose samples.
**Bring** the frayed sample to the union branch meeting on paid checks.
feel: **Calm** about current shifts and family money.
S0.quote: A hose that splits at the coupling can ruin a machine far from our factory.
fieldNote: Omar **never uses AI** and places safety evidence from a cut hose above the office order list.
His **union branch action** is concrete, while four months saved and regular pay support his calm response.

steps.text: Keep setting hose braid tension and cutting changeover samples
Bring frayed hose sample to union branch meeting about paid checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write orders and plan deliveries before robots take the hose off a reel. The company should tell us what it buys before it tells us to run faster. I'd ask the union branch to demand paid instruction for any new machine duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hands-on work changes more slowly, but the night shift could lose hours if orders are scheduled differently. Four months saved gives us time, not permission to ignore a smaller wage. My partner's library pay covers some bills, not all of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the branch rep to put a written roster and paid safety instruction on next month's meeting agenda. I'll keep the hose line running and compare the new roster with the last three pay slips. If a trainer-led course on a new guard system is required and offered on paid time, I'll attend; I won't buy a private AI course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can cope with a new guard, but a shortened roster would need a proper household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe guard training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to isolate the braider, open the guard and check that the wire reel cannot turn before I reach inside. A trainer must watch me do it on a stopped machine. A slide presentation cannot teach a safe hand position beside the hose braider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which roster number matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our last three slips show the base shift plus occasional overtime. I would compare base hours first, because overtime is not promised. If base hours actually fall, I would ask the branch to challenge the roster.

say: **AI scheduling** may change paid shifts before robots handle hose reels.
The **union branch** should demand a written roster and paid safety teaching.
think: My **hands-on job** changes slowly, but base hours might shrink.
A **four-month reserve** helps, though library pay cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: **Raise** roster and paid instruction at the next union branch meeting.
**Compare** posted base shifts with three pay slips.
**Attend** required new-guard course if a paid trainer-led place is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about possible base-hour loss despite present savings.
S1.quote: A slide presentation cannot teach a safe hand position beside the hose braider.
fieldNote: His **resistance to AI** does not stop him accepting required paid instruction on a physical guard.
He distinguishes **base hours** from uncertain overtime before calling a new roster a real wage cut.

steps.text: Raise written base roster and paid guard instruction at union branch
Compare posted base shifts with last three pay slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch that thinking AI could plan hose orders by 2028, and capable robots around 2031 could braid, cut and inspect them. I would ask the employer for a written headcount plan while there are still people to negotiate with. I don't need to pretend the robot has been ordered already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when physical robots could do the line work. I expect a major cut to braiding shifts, and four months saved will not cover years of mortgage payments. My partner's library job helps, but two children still need meals and school costs. I have been awake thinking through the pay gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union branch to meet management this month about notice, wage protection and funded paid practical training. If the plant offers a real guarded hose-inspection apprenticeship with fees and paid time covered, I'll take the place. If my base hours are cut, I'll apply for posted safe local factory jobs with regular pay enough for the mortgage; after qualifying, I'll also apply for posted local hose-inspection openings under the same safety and pay terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can point to a damaged hose, but I cannot point to a guaranteed second wage when a robot takes the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to management talks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the last roster and the first cut sample with a broken wire to the branch meeting. The roster shows the money at risk; the sample shows the inspection job still has safety duties. I want both in the written deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What separates a course from a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course place has to be offered, paid and taught beside a guarded machine. Then a posted inspection vacancy has to exist and cover the mortgage without counting overtime. I would not leave my hose-braiding wage on a training brochure alone.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes hose orders before capable robots reach braiding around 2031.
Our **union branch** should bargain for notice, wages and paid practical training.
think: At **48**, I expect major cuts to braiding shifts.
Four months of **savings** cannot cover years of mortgage and school costs.
do: **Meet** management through the branch for written notice and wage terms.
**Attend** funded paid guarded inspection apprenticeship if a place opens.
**Apply** for posted safe local factory or qualified inspection work if hours cut and pay fits.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless pay-gap worries.
S2.quote: I would not leave my hose-braiding wage on a training brochure alone.
fieldNote: He expects **major hour loss** by 2031 and describes lost sleep despite four months saved.
His **factory fallback** and qualified inspection application require separate real local postings, safe duties and sufficient regular pay.

steps.text: Ask union branch to negotiate written notice, wages and paid training
Attend guarded hose-inspection apprenticeship if funded paid place offered
Apply for posted safe local factory role if base hours cut and pay covers mortgage
Apply for posted safe local inspection if qualified, base hours cut and pay covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI might plan orders in 2031 and capable robots could handle the braiders around 2034. Five years is enough to bargain before the machines reach the floor. I'd ask our branch to put real paid training seats beside the wage terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when physical robots reach the reels. The children will be older, though the mortgage may remain. We could add to our reserve if full wages continue, but a course without a posted job would not settle the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take any offered extra paid Saturday shift and put the new wage into our reserve after bills. At the branch meeting I'll press for a funded paid certificate in hose testing with supervised guard practice. If the plant offers a real place, I'll enrol; once qualified, if braiding hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local testing roles only where base pay covers our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about future hours, but I can use the years to ask for terms in writing. I don't need a new app to read a wage line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the practical test include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should include a burst-pressure gauge, a bad coupling and a stopped reel. I want to know how to reject a hose before it reaches a customer's machine. Someone qualified must watch the practical test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What rate would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The testing vacancy has to show its base rate and regular shift. The library job cannot cover the mortgage if I take a large cut. I would keep braiding while I looked for a posting that fits.

Our branch should seek **paid testing seats** alongside wage protection.

S3.quote: I want to know how to reject a hose before it reaches a customer's machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan hose orders by 2036, while capable robots might braid and test around 2039. Ten years lets workers and employers agree on shorter hours and wages before the hardware arrives. Our union branch should start that discussion while the factory still has orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when the physical robots arrive. The children may be grown, but the mortgage and living costs could still need my wage. Four months saved now is useful, and the plant's typical pay gives me room to prepare if full shifts last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the hose job and pay extra mortgage principal from any offered paid overtime after household bills. I'll attend the branch's quarterly bargaining meetings about paid roles and notice. If the employer offers a funded paid practical qualification in machine safety, with a supervised guarded place, I'll take it; after qualifying, if the line cuts my hours, I'll apply only for posted safe local jobs with regular pay enough for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end of it. Ten years lets me test a real course and a real wage before I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a future safety job need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The employer would need to show which paid safety posts remain and who holds stop authority when a hose fails pressure testing. A machine-safety certificate with no actual work attached would not cover the mortgage. I want the posting in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay extra on the loan immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my partner and I would count the coming month's bills first. Only wages from an offered extra shift beyond those bills would go against the loan. The four months already saved stay ready for a broken van or a lost shift.

The **union branch** should bargain over paid roles and notice while orders continue.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut the braiding shifts that pay our mortgage. Written notice and wage terms, an offered funded paid practical course, and a safe posted local role at enough base pay would help. I'd want the branch at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the pressure test after a robot braids the hose. A pressure hose can look perfect on a screen and still burst at a bad coupling.

headlineQuote: A pressure hose can look perfect on a screen and still burst at a bad coupling.
portrait: **Omar**, 43, operates a steel-wire hose braider with a vocational certificate, typical pay and four months saved.
He and his library-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with some similar factories nearby.
His **progressive outlook** leads to actual union branch bargaining, while he never uses AI and favors paid hands-on instruction.
Fast robots make him **alarmed** about lost braiding wages; he needs real training places and posted safe local work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable braiding robots around 2031 and cut mortgage-paying shifts.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid practical training and a posted safe local job at enough base pay would help.
